join.title: Find the total order amount for each customer and their last order date
join.description:
In a small retail company, there are two main tables: `customers` and `orders`. The `customers` table contains information about each customer such as their name and address. The `orders` table contains details about the orders placed by each customer, including the order amount and the order date. The task is to find the total order amount for each customer and their most recent order date. The query should also exclude any customers who have not placed any orders.

The objective is to generate a report showing each customer along with the total amount they have spent and the date of their latest order. If a customer has made multiple orders on the same day, the query should still show only one record per customer with the most recent order date.

Rules and constraints include: NULL order amounts should be treated as 0, results should be ordered by customer ID, and only customers with at least one order should be included in the final output.
constraints: Results must be ordered by customer_id ASC
NULL values in the amount column should be treated as 0
Only include customers who have placed at least one order
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Think about how the tables relate to each other, specifically focusing on the relationship between `customers` and `orders`.
Consider what aggregation or filtering is needed to get the total amount spent and the last order date for each customer.
Think about edge cases like NULL values and ensure the query handles them appropriately.
join.reference_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spent, MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order_date FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 0 ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;

join.title: Find Users Who Have Made Transactions on Multiple Days in a Month
join.description:
In a financial application, you need to identify all users who have made transactions on multiple days within a single month. This helps in identifying active users who engage frequently in transactions.

The query should return a list of user IDs and the count of distinct transaction days for each user in the given month. The result should include users who made at least 2 transactions on different days within the month.

Users with no transactions during the month should not be included in the results. If a user has made transactions on the same day, it should not be counted towards the distinct transaction days.
constraints: Results must be ordered by distinct_days DESC
NULL values in transaction_date should be treated as 0 and not included in the count
Only include users who have made transactions on more than one day in the month
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Start by joining the users and transactions tables on the user_id column
Use aggregation functions to count the distinct transaction days for each user
Filter out users who do not meet the requirement of having transactions on more than one day
join.reference_query: SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT t.transaction_date) AS distinct_days FROM users u JOIN transactions t ON u.user_id = t.user_id WHERE t.transaction_date BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-10-31' GROUP BY u.user_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT t.transaction_date) > 1;

join.title: Projects and Teams Join Query
join.description:
In a software company, there are multiple projects and teams. Each project can have one team assigned to it, and each team has several members. The goal is to find out which teams are working on more than one project and their total number of projects. The query should also include the team name, the total number of projects, and the team leader’s name. If a team leader is not specified, it should be treated as 'Unknown'.

The query must return the team name, the count of projects each team is working on, and the team leader’s name. If there is no team leader, the leader’s name should be shown as 'Unknown'.

Team names should be listed in descending order of the number of projects they are working on. In case of a tie, list them alphabetically by team name.
constraints: Results must be ordered by num_projects DESC, then by team_name ASC
NULL values in the leader_name field should be treated as 'Unknown'
Include only teams working on more than one project
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Think about how the teams and projects tables are related to each other
Consider what aggregation is needed to count the projects each team is working on
Think about how to handle NULL values in the leader_name column
join.reference_query: SELECT t.team_name, COUNT(p.project_id) AS num_projects, COALESCE(t.leader_name, 'Unknown') AS leader_name FROM teams t LEFT JOIN projects p ON t.team_id = p.team_id GROUP BY t.team_name, t.leader_name ORDER BY num_projects DESC, t.team_name ASC;

join.title: Account Balances and Transfer History
join.description: In a financial institution, each account holder can have multiple bank accounts, and each account can have multiple transfers. The objective of this query is to find all bank accounts that had at least one transfer in the last month, along with the total number of transfers and the latest transfer amount. Additionally, the account holder's name should be included in the result set if it exists. If there are no transfers in the last month, the account should not appear in the results. The account holder’s name should be included if it is available, and the results should be ordered by the total number of transfers in descending order. If two accounts have the same number of transfers, then the account with the higher latest transfer amount should appear first. NULL values in the latest transfer amount should be treated as 0.
constraints: Results must be ordered by num_transfers DESC
NULL values in the latest transfer amount should be treated as 0
Include only records where there were at least one transfer in the last month
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Think about how the tables relate to each other, specifically the foreign key relationship between accounts and transfers
Consider what aggregation or filtering is needed to count the transfers and get the latest transfer amount
Think about edge cases like NULL values in the latest transfer amount and how they should be handled
join.reference_query: SELECT a.account_id, a.account_holder_name, COUNT(t.transfer_id) AS num_transfers, MAX(t.transfer_amount) AS latest_transfer_amount FROM accounts a LEFT JOIN transfers t ON a.account_id = t.account_id WHERE t.transfer_date >= '2023-08-15' GROUP BY a.account_id, a.account_holder_name HAVING COUNT(t.transfer_id) > 0 ORDER BY num_transfers DESC, latest_transfer_amount DESC;

join.title: Join Products and Categories
join.description:
In a retail company, there are two main tables: `products` and `categories`. The `products` table contains information about different products sold in the store, while the `categories` table contains information about the different categories these products belong to. Each product can belong to one category, and each category can have multiple products. The `product_id` in the `products` table corresponds to the `category_id` in the `categories` table.

Your task is to write a query that returns the name of each product along with the name of its corresponding category. The result should include all products and their categories. If a product does not have a corresponding category, it should still appear in the result with the category name set to 'Unknown'.

The output should be ordered by the product name in ascending order.
constraints: Results must be ordered by product_name ASC
NULL values in the category_name column should be treated as 'Unknown'
Include all products, even if they do not have a corresponding category
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Think about how the tables relate to each other, specifically using a LEFT JOIN to include all products.
Consider what aggregation or filtering is needed to handle products without a category.
Think about edge cases like products that do not have a corresponding category.
join.reference_query: SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(c.category_name, 'Unknown') AS category_name FROM products p LEFT JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id ORDER BY p.product_name ASC;

join.title: Sales Data by Region
join.description: In a retail company, there are multiple stores spread across different regions. Each store sells various products and generates sales. The goal is to find the total sales amount for each region. There are two main tables involved: `sales` which contains information about individual sales transactions, and `regions` which contains details about the sales regions. Each sale is associated with a region through the `region_id` field. The objective is to produce a report that shows the total sales amount for each region, sorted in descending order of the total sales amount.
constraints: Results must be ordered by total_sales DESC
NULL values in the sales amount should be treated as 0
Include only regions that have at least one sale
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Think about how the `sales` and `regions` tables are related through the `region_id` field
Consider using the `SUM` function to aggregate the sales amounts by region
Be mindful of handling NULL values in the sales amount column
join.reference_query: SELECT r.region_name, SUM(s.amount) AS total_sales FROM sales s JOIN regions r ON s.region_id = r.region_id GROUP BY r.region_name ORDER BY total_sales DESC;

join.title: Flight Passenger Join Query
join.description: A major airline company wants to analyze the number of passengers on each flight. They have two tables: `flights` which contains information about each flight, and `passengers` which contains details about each passenger who has boarded a flight. The goal is to determine the total number of passengers on each flight and display the flight number along with the count of passengers for each flight. Passengers may board multiple flights, but each flight can only have one flight number.
constraints: Results must be ordered by flight_number ASC
NULL values should be treated as 0
Include only records where passenger_id is not null
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Think about how the `flights` and `passengers` tables relate to each other
Consider what aggregation or filtering is needed to get the correct count of passengers
Think about edge cases like NULL values and how they should be handled
join.reference_query: SELECT f.flight_number, COUNT(p.passenger_id) AS passenger_count FROM flights f LEFT JOIN passengers p ON f.flight_number = p.flight_number GROUP BY f.flight_number ORDER BY f.flight_number ASC;

join.title: Customer Orders
join.description: In a retail company, there are two main entities: Customers and Orders. Each order is made by a customer, and each customer can have multiple orders. The objective of this query is to find out which customers have placed at least one order and the total amount they have spent on all their orders. Additionally, it is important to note that if a customer has never placed an order, they should not appear in the result set. Also, any NULL values in the order amounts should be treated as zero, and the results should be sorted by the total spending in descending order.
constraints: Results must be ordered by total_spending DESC
NULL values in order_amount should be treated as 0
Only include customers who have placed at least one order
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Consider how the customer and order tables relate to each other
Think about using the appropriate join type and aggregate functions
Handle NULL values in the order_amount column appropriately
join.reference_query: SELECT c.customer_name, SUM(o.order_amount) AS total_spending FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name ORDER BY total_spending DESC;

join.title: Product Inventory Join Query
join.description: You are a retail store manager tasked with ensuring that the inventory levels for your products are always up-to-date. Your database contains two tables: `products` and `inventory`. The `products` table stores information about each product, including its unique identifier and name. The `inventory` table tracks the stock levels for each product and the last updated date. Your goal is to generate a report that shows the product name along with the current stock level and the last update date for each product. Additionally, you need to include only those products that have been updated within the last month. In case there are multiple updates for a product within the last month, you should choose the latest one.
constraints: Results must be ordered by last_update_date DESC
NULL values in stock_level should be treated as 0
Include only records where last_update_date is within the last month
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Consider how the `products` and `inventory` tables are related through the `product_id` field
Think about which fields you need to aggregate or filter to get the desired result
Handle the NULL values in `stock_level` appropriately before performing any calculations
join.reference_query: SELECT p.product_name, i.stock_level, i.last_update_date FROM products p JOIN inventory i ON p.product_id = i.product_id WHERE i.last_update_date >= '2023-02-01' ORDER BY i.last_update_date DESC;

join.title: Joining Products and Categories
join.description:
In an online retail store, there are multiple product categories and products that belong to these categories. The store owner wants to know which category has the highest total sales. Each product has a price and quantity sold, and the sales are calculated as the product of price and quantity sold. Your task is to write a query that returns the name of the category with the highest total sales. If multiple categories have the same total sales, return any one of them. 

The query should also include the total sales amount for each category, sorted in descending order by total sales. In case of ties in total sales, the category with the higher ID should be preferred. If the total sales amount is not available (i.e., it's NULL), treat it as zero for sorting purposes.

The categories and products are related such that the product belongs to exactly one category.
constraints: Results must be ordered by total_sales DESC
NULL values in total_sales should be treated as 0
In case of ties in total_sales, the category with the higher category_id should be preferred
join.starter_query:
-- Write your SQL query here

SELECT
hints: Consider the relationship between the categories and products tables and how they are linked through the category_id field.
Think about how to calculate the total sales for each category using appropriate aggregation functions.
For sorting and tie-breaking, consider the use of CASE statements or similar techniques.
join.reference_query: SELECT c.category_name, SUM(p.price * p.quantity_sold) AS total_sales FROM products p JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id GROUP BY c.category_name ORDER BY total_sales DESC LIMIT 1;
